passages.t: Paul, an apostle sent by Christ, who gave Himself for our sins
passages.happening:
Paul opens the letter the way letters opened in his day: who it is from, who it is to, and a greeting. But even this short opening argues.

He calls himself “Paul, an apostle—sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead” (verse 1). He writes with “all the brothers with me” (verse 2), and he writes “To the churches of Galatia” (verse 2). There is more than one church, in more than one town.

Then the greeting: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 3). And at once Paul says who Jesus is and what he did. He is the one “who gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father” (verse 4). Paul ends the opening with praise: “to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
An apostle is someone sent with a message, an envoy. Paul's first words answer a charge before anyone has made it aloud. Some in Galatia were saying that Paul had his message second-hand, from the leaders in Jerusalem, and had changed it. So Paul says at once that he was sent by Christ himself, and by the Father who raised him. The rest of chapters 1 and 2 will tell the story behind that claim.

Notice how quickly Paul says ‘raised Him from the dead’. For Paul the resurrection is not a later idea added to the faith. It is the fact everything stands on. The God who raised Jesus is the God who sent Paul.

‘Grace and peace’ joins a Greek greeting and a Jewish one. Greek letters usually began with a word that sounds like grace. Jewish greetings wished peace, shalom. Paul puts the two together and fills them with Christ.

Verse 4 sums up the whole gospel in one line. Christ ‘gave Himself’: no one took his life from him. He did it ‘for our sins’. And he did it ‘to rescue us’, the word used for pulling someone out of danger. Many Jews of Paul's day spoke of two ages, this present age and the age to come, when God would put the world right. Paul says that in Christ the new age has already broken in. Believers are rescued out of the old one even while they still live in it.

All of this, Paul says, was ‘according to the will of our God and Father’. The cross was not an accident or a defeat. It was God's own plan to save. The church confesses this as the heart of its faith: salvation is God's own act, by grace, through the death of his Son.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament gives Paul his language. ‘Grace and peace’ echoes the blessing of the priests: “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:25-26).

Christ ‘who gave Himself for our sins’ recalls the servant in Isaiah, who “poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12).

And the praise of verse 5 is the praise of the Psalms, which give glory to God and not to people: “Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory” (Psalm 115:1).
passages.asks: Paul cannot even say hello without talking about the cross. Ask what is at the centre of the way you speak about your faith. Is it what Christ gave, or what you do? And if Christ gave himself ‘for our sins’, ask whether you live as someone rescued, or as someone still trying to earn a rescue.

passages.happening:
Where Paul would usually give thanks for his readers, he does not. “I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel” (verse 6). Then he corrects himself: it is “not even a gospel” (verse 7). Some people are troubling them and trying to twist the good news of Christ.

Then Paul says the hardest words in the letter. “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse!” (verse 8). He says it twice (verse 9).

He finishes with a question. “Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God?” (verse 10). If he were still trying to please people, he says, he would not be a servant of Christ.
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would have noticed the missing thanksgiving straight away. The letter was read aloud in their gathering. In almost every other letter Paul thanks God for the people he writes to. The silence would have felt like a slap.

‘Deserting’ was a word for a soldier leaving his post, or someone changing sides. Paul does not say they are leaving him. He says they are leaving God, ‘the One who called you’.

‘Gospel’ means good news. In the Roman world the word was used for news of a victory or the birth of a ruler. Paul uses it for the news about Jesus. His point is that there is only one. The teachers in Galatia did not say they were bringing a new religion. They said they were adding to the gospel. Paul says that adding something to Christ as the price of belonging makes it another message altogether.

‘Under a curse’ is the Greek word anathema. In the Greek Old Testament it was used for something handed over to God, out of human hands. Notice who falls under it. Paul names himself first: ‘even if we’. Then an angel. The curse falls on a message, whoever brings it, not on a rival group.

Verse 10 answers another charge. Some said Paul made the gospel easy, leaving out circumcision so that Gentiles would like him. Paul says a man who calls down a curse like this is plainly not trying to be popular.
passages.ot:
The law of Moses had already taught Israel to test a message by its content, not by its messenger. If a prophet does a sign that comes true, but says, “Let us follow other gods (which you have not known) and let us worship them,” then “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer” (Deuteronomy 13:2-3). Paul says the same: not even an angel can change the message.

The word ‘good news’ comes from Isaiah, where messengers run to tell Zion that God has come to save. “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news” (Isaiah 52:7).

And Paul's refusal to please people stands in the line of the prophets, who spoke God's word when it made them unwelcome. God told Samuel, “the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.hard:
Is it not harsh for Paul to curse other teachers?

It is hard, and it should not be softened away. But it helps to see what Paul is and is not doing.

First, Paul thought the stakes were the gospel itself, not a matter of taste. To say that Gentiles must be circumcised to belong was, in his eyes, to say that Christ's death was not enough. He will say so plainly: “if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing” (2:21).

Second, Paul puts himself under the same curse if he ever changes the message. It is a line drawn around the gospel, not a weapon for one party.

Third, ‘let him be under a curse’ hands a person over to God's judgment. It is not a curse spoken in anger, and it is not permission for anyone to harm, shun or abuse the teachers. Paul tells the church to do none of those things. The site's note on 1 Corinthians 16:22 says the same about the curse at the end of that letter.

Fourth, Paul does not treat every disagreement this way. In Romans he tells believers who differ about food and holy days to welcome one another and not to judge (Romans 14). The line he draws here is at the gospel itself: Christ, crucified and risen, God's free gift, received by faith. Christians still have to think carefully about where that line falls in their own disputes. Most of what divides churches today is not this.

So this verse gives no one licence to curse the Christians they disagree with. It asks a harder thing: to care enough about the good news that we will not let anyone, ourselves included, change it.
passages.asks: Paul measured every message by what it says about Christ, not by who brings it. Ask what you add, quietly, to Christ as the price of belonging: a way of dressing, a style of worship, a political side, a list of rules. And ask whose approval you are working for. Paul says that if he were still trying to please people, he could not serve Christ.

passages.t: Called by God's grace: from persecutor to preacher
passages.happening:
Now Paul begins his story. “For I certify to you, brothers, that the gospel I preached was not devised by man” (verse 11). He did not receive it from anyone, nor was he taught it. “I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ” (verse 12).

They had heard about his past. “For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it” (verse 13). He was ahead of others of his age, and “extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (verse 14).

Then God stepped in. God had set him apart from birth and called him by his grace, and “was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles” (verses 15-16). Paul did not hurry off to ask anyone's advice. He did not go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who came before him. Instead, “I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Paul's point in telling his story is simple. If his message had come from the leaders in Jerusalem, his critics could say he had learned it badly. So he shows how little time he spent with them. His gospel came from Christ himself.

‘Judaism’ here means the Jewish way of life, kept with great care. Paul was not a careless Jew who never understood his faith. He was among the most devoted. Elsewhere he calls himself “a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee” (Philippians 3:5). The Pharisees were a movement of Jews who kept the law and its traditions with great care.

‘Zealous’ is a strong word. In Jewish memory zeal recalled heroes such as Phinehas, who acted with force against those who broke God's covenant. Paul's zeal for God is what drove him to persecute the church. He thought he was defending God.

That is what makes verse 15 so striking. Paul does not say he worked his way out of his error. He says God ‘called me by His grace’. The man who was destroying the church did nothing to deserve this. Paul's own story is the gospel he preaches: grace to someone who did not earn it.

‘Reveal His Son in me’ may mean both that God showed Paul who Jesus is, and that God began to make Christ known through Paul's life. Acts tells the outward story, the light and the voice on the road near Damascus (Acts 9). Paul tells the inward one.

Arabia here most likely means the kingdom of the Nabataeans, east and south of Damascus. Its king, Aretas, later tried to have Paul arrested (2 Corinthians 11:32). What Paul did there, whether preaching, praying, or both, the letter does not say.
passages.ot:
Paul describes his call in the words God used to call the prophets. God said to Jeremiah, “before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jeremiah 1:5). Paul says God “set me apart from my mother’s womb” (verse 15), to preach among the nations.

The servant in Isaiah says the same: “The LORD called Me from the womb” (Isaiah 49:1). And God says to that servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Paul sees his own work among the Gentiles as part of that promise.

His old zeal recalls Phinehas, of whom God said, “he was zealous for My sake among them” (Numbers 25:11). Paul had thought he was following that example. Now he sees that zeal without knowledge led him to fight against God.
passages.hard:
Paul says he did not receive the gospel from any person. But in 1 Corinthians he writes, “For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3). Is that a contradiction?

Most readers think not. In Galatians Paul is speaking of the heart of his message and his call: that Jesus is the risen Son of God, and that Gentiles are welcome in him without the law. That he learned from the risen Christ himself, on the day he met him. In 1 Corinthians he is speaking of the church's shared summary of the facts, the death, burial, rising and appearances of Jesus, which he passed on in the words the church used. Paul could know Christ by revelation and still learn the church's words, the names of the witnesses and the stories of Jesus from those who came before him. The two letters agree on the message. They answer different questions.
passages.asks: Paul was most sure he was serving God on the day he was most wrong. Ask where your own zeal might be pointed at the wrong target. And notice how Paul tells his story: not as his own achievement, but as God's grace to someone who did not deserve it. If you belong to Christ, how would you tell your story that way?

passages.t: Fifteen days with Peter, and years in Syria and Cilicia
passages.happening:
“Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days” (verse 18). Paul saw none of the other apostles “except James, the Lord’s brother” (verse 19). Then he adds an oath: “I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie” (verse 20).

After that he went to “the regions of Syria and Cilicia” (verse 21). The churches in Judea did not know him by sight. They only heard the report: “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy” (verse 23). “And they glorified God because of me” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Cephas is the Aramaic name that Jesus gave to Simon, meaning rock. In Greek it is Peter. Paul uses both names in this letter.

Fifteen days is a short visit. That is Paul's point. He was not trained by Peter; he visited him. The word ‘confer’ can mean to get to know someone, or to ask questions of them. Paul surely heard much from Peter about Jesus in those days. But he did not get his gospel or his call from him.

‘Three years’ may be counted the way people counted then, with part of the first and part of the third year counting as years. So it could be a little under three full years.

James, ‘the Lord's brother’, was by this time a leader of the church in Jerusalem. During Jesus' ministry his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). The risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). Christians understand ‘brother’ in different ways: a son of Mary and Joseph, a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or a close relative. The site's note on Mark 3:31-35 sets out these readings and does not choose.

Why the oath in verse 20? Because Paul's critics were telling a different story about his past. He calls God as his witness that his account is true. Acts tells of the same visit with some differences: it says Barnabas brought Paul to the apostles, and that he left for Tarsus when his life was in danger (Acts 9:26-30). Paul says he saw only Peter and James among the apostles, and he is speaking under oath about exactly that.

Syria and Cilicia lay to the north. Paul's home town, Tarsus, was in Cilicia (Acts 22:3). He worked there for years before the story picks up again in chapter 2.

Verse 24 is a quiet sentence with great weight. Believers who had feared Paul, and had perhaps lost friends because of him, now praised God for him. They did not keep a list against him. They saw what God had done.
passages.ot:
Paul's oath, ‘before God’, follows the custom of Scripture, where a person who must be believed calls God as witness. Samuel said to Israel, “The LORD is a witness against you, and His anointed is a witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand” (1 Samuel 12:5).

And the churches of Judea ‘glorified God because of me’. Isaiah said that when God redeems his people, they will be “oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified” (Isaiah 61:3). A changed life brings glory to God, not to the one who was changed.
passages.asks: The churches who had been hurt by Paul glorified God when they heard he had changed. Ask whether there is someone whose change you find hard to believe, or hard to welcome. And ask whether your own life gives people a reason to praise God, not because you are impressive, but because they can see what grace has done.
